beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB/MongoDB connection string only from environment (process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI) or a secret store at runtime; never hard-code it or commit it to the repo. Provide a .env.example with a placeholder value only.

Use the official MongoDB Node.js driver (MongoClient) with unified topology and create a single shared MongoClient instance at app startup; reuse that client/connection pool across the process and only close it on graceful shutdown.

Set secure connection options: require TLS/SSL, enable retryable writes if supported, set reasonable timeouts (serverSelectionTimeoutMS, connectTimeoutMS), and configure maxPoolSize/minPoolSize to match expected concurrency.

Store secrets (DB credentials, LLM API keys) in a secret management service (Azure Key Vault) and inject them into the app at runtime rather than storing them in code or plain .env files; rotate credentials periodically.
Never log full connection strings, passwords or API keys. Redact or omit sensitive fields from logs and error messages (including stack traces that may contain env values).
Design an idempotent seed script: check for existence or use upsert/unique constraints so repeated runs do not create duplicate documents; make the seed script safe to run in CI and local dev.
Choose a partition/shard key that evenly distributes read/write load and aligns with common query patterns (for leads, consider companyId or a hashed leadId) to avoid hot partitions and RU spikes.

Model time-series or high-volume engagement signals in a separate collection (or capped/ttl collection) and keep lead master records relatively small; reference activity/embedding docs by leadId rather than embedding unbounded arrays into lead documents.

Create indexes that match your read patterns: index leadId, companyId, lastActivityDate, and any fields used in filters/sorts. For any fields used only in projections for the LLM prompt, still prefer fetching only those fields (use projection).

For vector search, store vectors with explicit metadata (dimension, dtype) and create a vector index (HNSW/IVF) tuned for the desired recall/latency (parameters like efConstruction, M, ef); normalize vectors consistently before indexing and querying.

Limit documents returned to the fields needed to build the LLM prompt (projection) to reduce data transfer and RU consumption; avoid fetching large binary fields or full activity blobs when only summaries are required.

Use query explain() / the provider's profiler to validate that queries use the intended indexes and to measure RU/IO cost; iterate and add compound indexes when necessary for frequent multi-field queries.

Implement optimistic concurrency control when updating lead documents (e.g., include a version field or use findOneAndUpdate with conditional filter) so scoring writes do not inadvertently clobber concurrent changes.

When performing multi-document multi-collection updates that must be atomic (rare for lead scoring), use database transactions only if the MongoDB API on the cluster supports them; otherwise design updates to be idempotent and compensating.

Implement exponential-backoff and jitter for transient errors and throttling (HTTP 429 / MongoNetworkError / transient network issues). Respect Retry-After where provided and limit total retries for idempotent vs non-idempotent ops.

Prefer built-in driver retryable reads/writes if available, but still implement application-level retry/backoff for operations that may not be retry-safe (e.g., LLM call + write sequence — design for idempotency or store an operation log to deduplicate).

Enforce collection-level schema validation (JSON Schema validators) for lead documents to ensure required fields (leadId, companyId, createdAt, etc.) and types are present; reject malformed data early.

Use least-privilege database users/roles for the app: create a DB user that can read and update only the specific database/collections required (no admin privileges). Rotate DB credentials regularly and audit usage.

Protect PII before sending data to the LLM: minimize text, redact or hash sensitive identifiers if not required for scoring, and record consent/processing policies. Log only non-sensitive metadata about LLM calls.

Guard LLM calls behind feature flags, quotas, and validation: validate prompts and inputs before sending, rate-limit calls, and fall back to deterministic scoring rules when the LLM or API key is unavailable.

When updating a lead document with the score and rationale, use an atomic update operation (findOneAndUpdate with $set) and include metadata (scoredAt, scorerId, modelVersion) so you can trace how/when the score was created.
Use TTL (expireAfterSeconds) indexes for ephemeral engagement data or temp caches to automatically remove old signals and control storage/RU costs.
Instrument and monitor RU consumption, operation latency, index usage, error rates and throttles; set alerts for RU spikes and 429 rates so you can scale or tune indexes/queries proactively.
Avoid doing expensive full-collection scans during request handling; paginate results, use capped queries, and limit result sizes so the scoring endpoint remains responsive under load.

Store vector indexes and heavy-weight ML artifacts in a separate collection or namespace and tune their resource provisioning separately; when possible, provision enough compute (instance class/cluster tier) for anticipated vector search throughput.
